project.name: Pocket Tasks
project.title: Design proposals
project.description: Options for the first-run experience, built on their own branches from the same base and compared on the same screens (412x915 phone, 1440x900 desktop, fresh browser profile).

proposals.title: First-run experience for new users
proposals.brief:
Decide what a first-time user sees on an empty Pocket Tasks. Comes from idea *i-1* (go) and *i-3* (maybe).

**Constraints:** no backend, no new dependencies, under 30 changed lines, nothing new for returning users with tasks. Every option starts from the same base commit, where a new user's list is empty.

criteria.label: First task without help
criteria.description: How clearly the screen says what to do first.

criteria.label: Accessible
criteria.description: WCAG 2.2 AA: labels, focus, dismissal, reflow at 320 px.

criteria.label: Stays out of the way
criteria.description: No clutter or leftovers once the user has their own tasks.

criteria.label: Small to build and keep
criteria.description: Changed lines, state to persist, cases to test.

recommendation.reasoning:
It scores highest on the two heaviest criteria: the help sits in the empty list where the user is already looking (research r-1), and it is the only option that also fixes the unlabeled field. It needs no stored state, so there is nothing to get out of sync.

Its weakness is that it teaches only adding a task, not ticking or deleting. Pick **sample tasks** instead if usage data later shows new users not discovering the checkbox; pick neither of the others for a coach mark, which failed on the phone screenshot.

options.title: Teaching empty state
options.summary: When the list is empty, a dashed panel says *Nothing to do yet* and how to add a task. Also adds the visible **New task** label from idea i-2.
options.reasoning: Help in context, driven by state rather than a stored flag: it shows exactly when the list is empty and never otherwise.
pros: Help sits where the user looks first
cons: Teaches adding only, not ticking or deleting
Shows again whenever a user clears the list

clarity.note: Heading plus one sentence; the label names the field.

a11y.note: Visible label; plain text in the flow; nothing to dismiss.

clean.note: Gone as soon as one task exists.

options.evidence: Checked in Chromium at 412x915 and 1440x900 with an empty profile: the panel renders below the form and hides after adding a task. No tests exist in this example app.

options.title: Three sample tasks
options.summary: On first run the list holds three italic sample tasks whose text explains ticking, adding and deleting. A `localStorage` flag makes sure they appear once.
options.reasoning: Learning by doing: the user's first tap can be ticking a sample, and they see a populated list straight away.
pros: Shows what a full list looks like
cons: The count says *3 left* for tasks the user never made
Users must delete the samples by hand
Still no label on the add field

clarity.note: Clear, but the user may not realise the tasks are examples.

a11y.note: Italic grey text is readable, but the unlabeled field remains.

clean.note: Leaves three tasks and a wrong count to clean up.

cost.note: 10 lines plus one storage key to reason about.

options.title: Dismissible coach mark
options.summary: A dark callout under the add field says *Start here* with a **Got it** button; Escape also closes it, and a `localStorage` flag keeps it closed.
options.reasoning: Points straight at the one control that matters, and goes away for good once dismissed.
cons: On a 412 px phone the **Got it** button is pushed off screen by the fixed-width form
One more state to persist and test
Still no label on the add field
